readings.c1s1:
welde, < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''welde'', < AS. ''wylde'', powerful, < ''wealdan'', wield: see ''wield''.] Weak; impotent.
{{smaller block|<poem>The more he preyseth Eelde,
Though he be croked and ''unweelde''.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 4886.}}}}

'''unwieldily''' (un-wēl′di-li), ''adv.'' In an unwieldy manner; cumbrously. ''Dryden.''

'''unwieldiness''' (un-wēl′di-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unwieldy; heaviness; difficulty of being moved: as, the ''unwieldiness'' of a person having a corpulent body. ''Donne'', Love’s Diet.

'''unwieldsome†''' (un-wēld′sum), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wieldsome''.] Unwieldy. ''North'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 582.

'''unwieldy''' (un-wēl′di), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''unweldie''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wieldy''.] Movable or moving with difficulty; unmanageable from size, shape, or weight; lacking pliability: as, an ''unwieldy'' hulk; an ''unwieldy'' rock.
{{smaller block|Bestow on him some more heart, for that grosse and so ''unweldie'' a body.
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 340.}}
Public business, in its whole ''unwieldy'' compass, must always form the subject of these daily chronicles.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Style, i.}}}}

'''unwild†''' (un-wīld′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''wild''<sup>1</sup>.] To tame. ''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., Handie-Crafts. [Rare.]

'''unwilful''' (un-wil′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not wilful; not characterized by or done through wilfulness: as, an ''unwilful'' slight. ''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe, I. 8. (''Davies.'')

'''unwill''' (un-wil′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''will''<sup>1</sup>.] To will the reverse of; reverse one’s will in regard to.
readings.c1s3:
free from entanglement.

{{smaller block|In regard of them who desiring to serve God as they ought, but being not so skilful as in every point to ''unwind'' themselves where the snares of glossing speech do lie to entangle them. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. 4.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To admit of being unwound; become unwound: as, a skein that ''unwinds'' easily. ''Mortimer.''

¶
'''unwink†''' (un-wingk′), ''v. i.'' [ME. ''unwynken''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''wink.''] To open; unclose.

{{smaller block|<poem>When that thaire een gynneth forto ''unwynk''
And thai to brannche, into the lande let synk
A reede right by.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 105.}}}}

'''unwinking''' (un-wing′king), ''a.'' Not winking; not shutting the eyes; not ceasing to wake or watch.

{{smaller block|''Unwinking'' vigilance. {{right|''V. Knox'', Essays, No. 17.}}}}

'''unwinning''' (un-win′ing), ''a.'' Not winning; not adapted to win or gain favor; unconciliatory. ''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., II. ii. 7.

'''unwiped''' (un-wīpt′), ''a.'' Not wiped; not cleaned by rubbing. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, ii. 3. 108.

'''unwire''' (un-wīr′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''wire.''] To remove the wire of; take out the wire from. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|I must ''unwire'' that cage and liberate the captive. {{right|''Walter Colton'', Ship and Shore, p. 88.}}}}
readings.c2s1:
''unwisdom''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wisdom.''] Lack of wisdom; ignorance; foolishness; folly; unwise conduct or speech.
{{smaller block|Let us not commit the ''unwisdom'', rebuked ages ago by the highest voice, of disputing among ourselves which should be the greatest.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Amer. Lects., p. 98.}}}}

¶
'''unwise''' (un-wīz′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unwis'', < AS. ''unwīs'' (= OS. ''unwīs'' = OHG. MHG. ''unwīs'' = Goth. ''unveis''), unwise, foolish, ignorant, < ''un-'', not, + ''wīs'', wise: see ''un-''<sup>1</sup> and ''wise''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Not wise; Lacking wisdom or judgment; foolish; indiscreet: as, an ''unwise'' man; ''unwise'' kings. ''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 1. 91.—'''2.''' Not dictated by wisdom; not adapted to the desired end; injudicious; imprudent: as, ''unwise'' measures; ''unwise'' delay. ''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 1. 52.

'''unwisely''' (un-wīz′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''unwisely'', ''unwysely'', ''unwisliche'', < AS. ''unwīslīce'', unwisely; as ''unwise'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In an unwise manner; injudiciously; indiscreetly; not wisely; not prudently: as, ''unwisely'' rigid; ''unwisely'' studious.
{{smaller block|<poem>Saue thes fonnet folke, the frigies of troy,
That ''vnwysely'' has wroght with wyttis full febill,
And offendit our frenchyp thurgh foli of hom seluyn.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4207.}}}}

'''unwish†''' (un-wish′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''wish.''] To wish not to be; make away with by wishing. ''Shak.'', Hen. V., iv. 3. 76.

'''unwished''' (un-wisht′), ''a.'' Not wished for; not sought; not desired; unwelcome. ''Shak.'', M. N. D., i. 1. 81.

'''unwist†''' (un-wist′), ''a.'' [ME. ''unwist'', ''unwyst''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wist.''] '''1.''' Unknown; without being known.
readings.c2s2:
{{smaller block|''Unwist'' of every wyght but of Pandare.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 603.}}}}

'''2.''' Unknowing; ignorant.
{{smaller block|He shal the ese, ''unwyst'' of it hymselve.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 1400.}}}}

'''unwit†''' (un-wit′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unwiten''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wit'', ''v.''] To be ignorant.
{{smaller block|Whan that God knoweth anything to be, he ne ''unwot'' nat that thilke wantith necessite to be.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, v. prose 6.}}}}

'''unwit†''' (un-wit′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unwit'', ''unwitt'', ''onwit'', < AS. ''ungewit'', unwisdom, folly; as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wit'', ''n.''] Lack of wit; folly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hym wyte I that I dye,
And myn ''unwit'', that ever I clomb so hye.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Complaint of Mars, l. 271.}}}}

'''unwitch''' (un-wich′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''witch''.] To free from the effects of witchcraft; disenchant. ''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, iv. 7. [Rare.]

'''unwithdrawing''' (un-wiᴛ̵ʜ-drâ′ing), ''a.'' Not withdrawing; continually liberal.
{{smaller block|Such a full and ''unwithdrawing'' hand.
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 711.}}}}

'''unwithered''' (un-wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėrd), ''a.'' Not withered or faded.
{{smaller block|The yet ''unwither’d'' blush.
{{right|''Shirley'' (''and Fletcher''?), Coronation, v.}}}}

'''unwithering''' (un-wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ing), ''a.'' Not liable to wither or fade. ''Cowper'', Task, iii. 570.

'''unwithheld''' (un-wiᴛ̵ʜ-held′), ''a.'' Not withheld; not kept or held back; not hindered. ''Thomson'', To Sir Isaac Newton.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''unwithstood''' (un-wiᴛ̵ʜ-stůd′), ''a.'' Not opposed or resisted. ''J. Philips'', Cider, i.

'''unwitnessed''' (un-wit′nest), ''a.'' Not witnessed; not attested by witnesses; wanting testimony. ''Hooker.''

'''unwittily''' (un-wit′i-li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''unwittili''; < ''unwitty'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Without wit; not wittily. ''Cowley.''

'''unwitting†''' (un-wit′ing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unwittinge''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''witting'', ''n.''] Ignorance.
{{smaller block|And now, bretheren, I woot that by ''unwiting'' ȝee diden.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Acts iii. 17.}}}}

'''unwitting''' (un-wit′ing), ''a.'' [Formerly also ''unweeting''; < ME. ''unwittyng'', ''unwityng'', ''unwetyng'', ''onwitinde'', < AS. ''unwitend'' (= OHG. ''unwizzende'' = Icel. ''ūvitandi''); as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''witting'', ''a.''] Not knowing; ignorant.
{{smaller block|''Unwittyng'' of this Dorigen at al.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Franklin’s Tale, l. 208.}}
<poem>Children that, ''unwitting'' why,
Lent the gay shout their shrilly cry.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., iii. 20.}}}}

'''unwittingly''' (un-wit′ing-li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''unwittyngly'', ''unwetandli''; < ''unwitting'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Without knowing; ignorantly. ''Chaucer.''
{{smaller block|They run from my pen ''unwittingly'', if they be verse.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, i. 1.}}}}

'''unwitty''' (un-wit′i), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unwitti'' (= OHG. ''unwizzig'' = Icel. ''ūvitugr''); < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''witty''.] '''1†.'''
readings.c3s1:
dom iii. 12.—'''2.''' Not witty; destitute of wit: as, ''unwitty'' jokes. ''Shenstone'', A Simile.

'''unwived†''' (un-wīvd′), ''a.'' Having no wife. ''Selden.''

'''unwoman''' (un-wu̇m′a̤n), ''v. t.'' To deprive of the qualities of a woman; unsex. ''Sandys'', tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., ii.

'''unwomanly''' (un-wu̇m′a̤n-li), ''a.'' Not womanly; unbecoming a woman; unfeminine.
{{smaller block|<poem>A woman sat, in ''unwomanly'' rags,
Plying her needle and thread.</poem>
{{right|''Hood'', Song of the Shirt.}}}}

'''unwomanly''' (un-wu̇m′a̤n-li), ''adv.'' In a manner unbecoming a woman.
{{smaller block|For your poor children’s sake, do not so ''unwomanly'' cast away yourself. ''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, ii.}}

'''unwonder†''' (un-wun′dėr), ''v. t.'' To deprive of wonder; explain so as to make no longer a wonder or marvel.
{{smaller block|Whilest Papists crie up this his incredible continency, others easily ''unwonder'' the same, by imputing it partly to his impotence afflicted with an infirmitie, partly to the distaste of his wife.
{{right|''Fuller'', Church Hist., II. vi. 17. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unwondering''' (un-wun′dėr-ing), ''a.'' Not wondering; incurious.
{{smaller block|<poem>But, wiser now, the ''unwondering'' world, alas!
Gives all poor Herschel’s glory to his glass.</poem>
{{right|''Wolcot'' (Peter Pindar), p. 236.}}}}

'''unwont†''' (un-wunt′), ''a.'' Unwonted; unaccustomed.
{{smaller block|''Unwont'' with heards to watch, or pasture sheepe.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. xi. 40.}}}}

'''unwonted''' (un-wun′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not wonted; not common; uncommon; unusual; infre-
readings.c3s2:
quent; rare: as, an ''unwonted'' sight; ''unwonted'' changes. ''Dryden.''
{{smaller block|<poem>And joy ''unwonted'', and surprise,
Gave their strange wildness to his eyes.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, vi. 5.}}}}
'''2.''' Unaccustomed; unused; not made familiar by practice: as, a child ''unwonted'' to strangers. ''Milton.''

'''unwontedly''' (un-wun′ted-li), ''adv.'' In an unwonted or unaccustomed manner.

'''unwontedness''' (un-wun′ted-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unwonted; uncommonness; rareness. ''Jer. Taylor'' (?), Artificial Handsomeness, p. 121.

'''unwooed''' (un-wöd′), ''a.'' Not wooed; not courted. ''Shak.'', Sonnets, liv.

'''unwoof''' (un-wöf′), ''v. t.'' To remove the woof of. [Rare.]

'''unworded''' (un-wėr′ded), ''a.'' Not worded; not spoken, told, or mentioned; also, not speaking; silent.
{{smaller block|<poem>You should have found my thanks paid in a smile
If I had fell ''unworded.''</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Nice Valour, ii. 1.}}
<poem>So, still ''unworded'', save in memory mute,
Rest thou, sweet hour of viol and of lute.</poem>
{{right|''R. W. Gilder'', Lyrics, Music and Words.}}}}

'''unwork''' (un-wėrk′), ''v. t.'' To undo.
{{smaller block|If they light in the middle or bottom of a dead hedge, your best way is softly to ''unwork'' the hedge till you come to them. ''C. Butler'', Fem. Mon., p. 92. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}

'''unworkable''' (un-wėr′ka-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not workable; not capable of being wrought into shape. —'''2.''' Hard to manage or to induce to work; indocile.
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|I think it would be difficult to find a body more ''unworkable'', or more difficult to bring together or to manage.
{{right|''Lancet'', No. 3522, p. 505.}}}}

'''unworking''' (un-wėr′king), ''a.'' Living without labor: as, the ''unworking'' classes. ''J. S. Mill.''

'''unworkmanlike''' (un-wėrk′man-līk), ''a.'' Not workmanlike; unlike what a good workman would make or do.
{{smaller block|Some of the most inartistic and ''unworkmanlike'' of the products have proudly been pointed to by school commissioners as proofs of the success of the manual-training course.
{{right|''New York Evening Post'', April 25, 1891.}}}}

'''unworld''' (un-wėrld′), ''v. t.'' To cause not to be worldly or to belong to the world. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Take away the least vericulum out of the world, and it ''unworlds'' all.
{{right|''N. Ward'', Simple Cobler, p. 21.}}}}

'''unworldliness''' (un-wėrld′li-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unworldly.

'''unworldly''' (un-wėrld′li), ''a.'' Not worldly; not influenced by worldly or sordid motives; spiritual.

'''unwormed''' (un-wėrmd′), ''a.'' Not wormed; not having the worm-like lytta cut from under the tongue: said of a dog.
{{smaller block|<poem>She is mad with love,
As mad as ever ''unworm’d'' dog was.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Woman Pleased, iv. 3.}}}}

'''unworn''' (un-wōrn′), ''a.'' Not worn; not impaired. ''Burke.''

'''unwilled''' (un-wild′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Deprived of the faculty of will; bereft of the power of volition. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Now, your will is all ''unwilled.''
{{right|''Mrs. Browning'', Duchess May.}}}}
'''2.''' Not willed; not purposed; involuntary; unintentional; spontaneous. ''Clarke.''

'''unwilling''' (un-wil′ing), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not willing; loath; disinclined; reluctant: as, an ''unwilling'' servant.
{{smaller block|If the sun rise ''unwilling'' to his race. {{right|''Dryden.''}}
<poem>The next came Nedham in on lusty horse,
That, angry with delay, at trumpet’s sound,
Would snort, and stamp, and stand upon no ground,
''Unwilling'' of his master’s tarriance. ''Peele'', Polyhymnia.</poem>}}
'''2†.''' Undesigned; involuntary.
{{smaller block|Patience, I pray you; ’twas a fault ''unwilling.''
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iv. 1. 159.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' Opposed, averse, indisposed, backward.}}

'''unwillingly''' (un-wil′ing-li), ''adv.'' In an unwilling manner; against one’s will; not with good will; reluctantly. ''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 368.

'''unwillingness''' (un-wil′ing-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unwilling; loathness; disinclination; reluctance. ''Shak.'', Rich. III., ii. 2. 92.

'''unwily''' (un-wī′li), ''a.'' Not wily; free from cunning. ''Eclectic Rev.''

''trans.'' '''1.''' To wind off; loose or separate, as what is wound or convolved; set free or loose: as, to ''unwind'' thread or a ball.—'''2.''' To disentangle; free from entanglement.

{{smaller block|In regard of them who desiring to serve God as they ought, but being not so skilful as in every point to ''unwind'' themselves where the snares of glossing speech do lie to entangle them. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. 4.}}}}

{{right|''Shirley'' (''and Fletcher''?), Coronation, v.}}}}

'''unwithering''' (un-wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ing), ''a.'' Not liable to wither or fade. ''Cowper'', Task, iii. 570.

'''unwithheld''' (un-wiᴛ̵ʜ-held′), ''a.'' Not withheld; not kept or held back; not hindered. ''Thomson'', To Sir Isaac Newton.

'''unwithstood''' (un-wiᴛ̵ʜ-stůd′), ''a.'' Not opposed or resisted. ''J. Philips'', Cider, i.

'''unwitnessed''' (un-wit′nest), ''a.'' Not witnessed; not attested by witnesses; wanting testimony. ''Hooker.''

'''unwittily''' (un-wit′i-li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''unwittili''; < ''unwitty'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Without wit; not wittily. ''Cowley.''

'''unwitting†''' (un-wit′ing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unwittinge''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''witting'', ''n.''] Ignorance.
{{smaller block|And now, bretheren, I woot that by ''unwiting'' ȝee diden.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Acts iii. 17.}}}}

'''unwitting''' (un-wit′ing), ''a.'' [Formerly also ''unweeting''; < ME. ''unwittyng'', ''unwityng'', ''unwetyng'', ''onwitinde'', < AS. ''unwitend'' (= OHG. ''unwizzende'' = Icel. ''ūvitandi''); as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''witting'', ''a.''] Not knowing; ignorant.
{{smaller block|''Unwittyng'' of this Dorigen at al.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Franklin’s Tale, l. 208.}}
<poem>Children that, ''unwitting'' why,
Lent the gay shout their shrilly cry.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., iii. 20.}}}}

'''unwittingly''' (un-wit′ing-li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''unwittyngly'', ''unwetandli''; < ''unwitting'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Without knowing; ignorantly. ''Chaucer.''
{{smaller block|They run from my pen ''unwittingly'', if they be verse.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, i. 1.}}}}

'''unwitty''' (un-wit′i), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unwitti'' (= OHG. ''unwizzig'' = Icel. ''ūvitugr''); < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''witty''.] '''1†.''' dom iii. 12.—'''2.''' Not witty; destitute of wit: as, ''unwitty'' jokes. ''Shenstone'', A Simile.

'''unwived†''' (un-wīvd′), ''a.'' Having no wife. ''Selden.''

'''unwoman''' (un-wu̇m′a̤n), ''v. t.'' To deprive of the qualities of a woman; unsex. ''Sandys'', tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., ii.

'''unwomanly''' (un-wu̇m′a̤n-li), ''a.'' Not womanly; unbecoming a woman; unfeminine.
{{smaller block|<poem>A woman sat, in ''unwomanly'' rags,
Plying her needle and thread.</poem>
{{right|''Hood'', Song of the Shirt.}}}}

'''unwomanly''' (un-wu̇m′a̤n-li), ''adv.'' In a manner unbecoming a woman.
{{smaller block|For your poor children’s sake, do not so ''unwomanly'' cast away yourself. ''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, ii.}}

'''unwonder†''' (un-wun′dėr), ''v. t.'' To deprive of wonder; explain so as to make no longer a wonder or marvel.
{{smaller block|Whilest Papists crie up this his incredible continency, others easily ''unwonder'' the same, by imputing it partly to his impotence afflicted with an infirmitie, partly to the distaste of his wife.
{{right|''Fuller'', Church Hist., II. vi. 17. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unwondering''' (un-wun′dėr-ing), ''a.'' Not wondering; incurious.
{{smaller block|<poem>But, wiser now, the ''unwondering'' world, alas!
Gives all poor Herschel’s glory to his glass.</poem>
{{right|''Wolcot'' (Peter Pindar), p. 236.}}}}

'''unwont†''' (un-wunt′), ''a.'' Unwonted; unaccustomed.
{{smaller block|''Unwont'' with heards to watch, or pasture sheepe.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. xi. 40.}}}}

'''unwonted''' (un-wun′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not wonted; not common; uncommon; unusual; infrequent; rare: as, an ''unwonted'' sight; ''unwonted'' changes. ''Dryden.''
{{smaller block|<poem>And joy ''unwonted'', and surprise,
Gave their strange wildness to his eyes.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, vi. 5.}}}}
'''2.''' Unaccustomed; unused; not made familiar by practice: as, a child ''unwonted'' to strangers. ''Milton.''

'''unwontedly''' (un-wun′ted-li), ''adv.'' In an unwonted or unaccustomed manner.

'''unwontedness''' (un-wun′ted-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unwonted; uncommonness; rareness. ''Jer. Taylor'' (?), Artificial Handsomeness, p. 121.

'''unwooed''' (un-wöd′), ''a.'' Not wooed; not courted. ''Shak.'', Sonnets, liv.

'''unwoof''' (un-wöf′), ''v. t.'' To remove the woof of. [Rare.]

'''unworded''' (un-wėr′ded), ''a.'' Not worded; not spoken, told, or mentioned; also, not speaking; silent.
{{smaller block|<poem>You should have found my thanks paid in a smile
If I had fell ''unworded.''</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Nice Valour, ii. 1.}}
<poem>So, still ''unworded'', save in memory mute,
Rest thou, sweet hour of viol and of lute.</poem>
{{right|''R. W. Gilder'', Lyrics, Music and Words.}}}}

'''unwork''' (un-wėrk′), ''v. t.'' To undo.
{{smaller block|If they light in the middle or bottom of a dead hedge, your best way is softly to ''unwork'' the hedge till you come to them. ''C. Butler'', Fem. Mon., p. 92. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}

'''unworkable''' (un-wėr′ka-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not workable; not capable of being wrought into shape. —'''2.''' Hard to manage or to induce to work; indocile. {{smaller block|I think it would be difficult to find a body more ''unworkable'', or more difficult to bring together or to manage.
{{right|''Lancet'', No. 3522, p. 505.}}}}

'''unworking''' (un-wėr′king), ''a.'' Living without labor: as, the ''unworking'' classes. ''J. S. Mill.''

'''unworkmanlike''' (un-wėrk′man-līk), ''a.'' Not workmanlike; unlike what a good workman would make or do.
{{smaller block|Some of the most inartistic and ''unworkmanlike'' of the products have proudly been pointed to by school commissioners as proofs of the success of the manual-training course.
{{right|''New York Evening Post'', April 25, 1891.}}}}

'''unworld''' (un-wėrld′), ''v. t.'' To cause not to be worldly or to belong to the world. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Take away the least vericulum out of the world, and it ''unworlds'' all.
{{right|''N. Ward'', Simple Cobler, p. 21.}}}}

'''unworldliness''' (un-wėrld′li-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unworldly.

'''unworldly''' (un-wėrld′li), ''a.'' Not worldly; not influenced by worldly or sordid motives; spiritual.

'''unwormed''' (un-wėrmd′), ''a.'' Not wormed; not having the worm-like lytta cut from under the tongue: said of a dog.
{{smaller block|<poem>She is mad with love,
As mad as ever ''unworm’d'' dog was.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Woman Pleased, iv. 3.}}}}

'''unworn''' (un-wōrn′), ''a.'' Not worn; not impaired. ''Burke.''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
